answer: (English version) to the Commission Lynn Boylan (The Left) (10 April 2026) Subject: Export of live animals to war zones Haifa is the main entry point for livestock vessels arriving in Israel. Haifa is located in an area directly exposed to missile attacks. During the previous escalation, missile strikes occurred close to vessels unloading animals coming from the EU. Live animal exports have continued to Israel as conflict across the region escalates, endangering animals and workers. Article 3 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 (1) requires that no animal be transported in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering. Continuing exports to areas where hostilities are ongoing or likely to intensify is incompatible with this obligation. (2) Will the Commission: 1.

call on the Member States to suspend the export of live animals to Israel and other destinations in the Middle East affected by the current hostilities until the security situation has stabilised and compliance with EU animal welfare rules can be effectively guaranteed?
closely monitor vessels that have already departed and ensure that contingency measures are in place to prevent animals from being left in unsafe conditions?
assess systemic shortcomings that allow exports to proceed despite clearly foreseeable risks?

to the Commission Anja Hazekamp (The Left), Sebastian Everding (The Left) (13 April 2026) Subject: Suspension of animal shipments to conflict zones It is prohibited to transport animals in a way likely to cause injury or undue suffering to them (1). Nevertheless, animals are still being transported by sea from the EU to conflict zones. Events such as port closures, attacks on infrastructure or delays at sea lead to animals experiencing severe suffering or injury, and can even result in their death. Furthermore, these situations pose health and safety risks to crew members, port workers, drivers and veterinarians. The Ministry of Agriculture in the German state of Lower Saxony has recently banned the transport of cattle, sheep, goats and pigs to and through Bahrain, Iraq, Iran, Israel, Yemen, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, the Palestinian Territories, Saudi Arabia, Syria and the United Arab Emirates because the legal requirements cannot be met (2).

1. Can the Commission explain how it monitors the welfare of animals that have recently been transported by ship from the EU to conflict zones? 2. Is the Commission aware that, in order to ensure animal welfare, it is necessary for Member States to immediately suspend the export of live animals to regions with an unstable political situation? 3. Is the Commission prepared to adopt, by means of a delegated act, a list of countries outside the EU to which Member States may not export live animals for the reasons mentioned? Joint answer given by Mr Várhelyi on behalf of the European Commission (22 June 2026) The EU legislation on the protection of animals during transport (1) does not require the Commission to monitor directly the transport to conflict zones or to suspend exports to third countries. However, Member States’ competent authorities are responsible for enforcing the rules of this legislation. They can refuse approving long journeys for exports to third countries if there is no evidence that EU animal welfare rules will be respected for the entire journey to the destination. The Commission continues to audit Member States that transport animals by sea. Given the unstable situation in the Middle East, the Commission asked Member States to exceptionally issue replacement certificates for consignments when needed and reminded their obligation to ensure protection of animals during transport up to destination, including outside the EU. To improve animal welfare outside the EU, the Commission provides technical and financial support to the World Organisation for Animal Health and works to strengthen the application of its international animal welfare standards, including during transport. The Commission has no legal basis to adopt by means of delegated act a list of third countries to which animals may not be exported from Member States. The Commission’s proposal to revise EU rules on animal transport aimed at improving animal welfare during transport is currently with co-legislators.

Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 of 22 December 2004 on the protection of animals during transport and related operations and amending Directives 64/432/EEC and 93/119/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1255/97 (OJ L 3, 5.1.2005, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2005/1/oj ).
